opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a really tight connection there. The way I see it, the systems we'd want to help with alignment research aren't some exotic new kind of thing. They're going to look a lot like the language models we're already working with, just more capable. So a lot of the problems you have to solve to make them useful research assistants are the same problems we're already facing today.

Take something like InstructGPT. The core question was: how do you get a model to actually do what the person intends, rather than just continuing text in some plausible-sounding way? We used reinforcement learning from human feedback, and it turned out that a much smaller aligned model was preferred by people over a much bigger unaligned one. That tells you alignment isn't only a safety tax. It's often what makes the model useful in the first place. If you want a model that helps you with alignment research, you need it to follow your intent, be honest about what it does and doesn't know, and not make things up. Those are exactly the properties we're trying to get right now.

Then there's the evaluation problem, which I think is the crux. As tasks get harder, it gets harder for humans to tell whether the model did a good job. That's already true today for things like summarizing a long book or reviewing complex code. So we've been working on approaches like having models help humans evaluate other models' outputs, for example writing critiques that point out flaws a person might miss. That's essentially a small version of scalable oversight, and it's the same technique you'd need when the model is proposing alignment ideas that you can't easily verify on your own.

There's also a lot of practical learning. You find out where these methods break, what kinds of reward hacking show up, how models behave when they're slightly out of distribution, and you build up the infrastructure, the data pipelines, and the empirical intuitions. None of that is wasted. It's the foundation you'd build on.

And I think there's a nice asymmetry that makes me somewhat optimistic: evaluating research is generally easier than producing it. If we can get good enough at aligning systems so they're honest and genuinely trying to help, and get good at evaluating their outputs with AI assistance, then we can lean on them to do more and more of the actual alignment work. The goal isn't to solve alignment for superintelligence entirely by ourselves. It's to align the next system well enough that it can help us with the one after that. Working on current systems is how you take that first step and learn whether the step is actually sound.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is that the alignment problems we're facing right now with current systems are, in a lot of ways, smaller versions of the problems we'll face with much more capable systems. And so by solving the near-term problems, we're building up the toolkit, the techniques, the understanding that we need for the harder versions later.

But the more specific thing I'm excited about is this: if you can get a system like GPT-4 or whatever comes after it to be genuinely helpful and honest and to reliably do what you want, then you can start pointing it at alignment research itself. You can have it read papers, propose experiments, write code, critique ideas, help with interpretability, all of that. And the better aligned the system is, the more you can trust the output, and the more you can delegate to it.

So there's kind of a bootstrapping dynamic. The work we're doing now with RLHF, with scalable oversight, with trying to understand when models are being deceptive or sycophantic, that directly makes the models more useful as research assistants. And then those research assistants help us make progress on the next generation of alignment problems, which lets us build somewhat more capable systems that we also trust, and so on.

The crucial thing is that we don't need to solve the whole problem ourselves. We need to solve enough of it to get a system that's roughly as good as a human alignment researcher and that we can trust to do that kind of work. That's a much more tractable target than aligning a superintelligence directly. And in some sense, every technique we develop for current models is a bet that it'll carry over, or at least that the failure modes we find along the way will teach us what won't carry over.

I'd also say the practical work keeps us honest. It's easy to sit around and theorize about what alignment should look like, but when you actually try to get a real model to do the thing, you discover all the ways your assumptions were wrong. That empirical feedback loop is really valuable, and it's something we just didn't have a few years ago.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a fairly direct connection: if we want AI systems to help us with alignment research, we need to be able to get useful work out of them and evaluate whether that work is actually good. Working on aligning current systems gives us practice with both of those things.

For example, you could start with a system that helps you write code for experiments, or critiques an experimental design, or finds problems in an argument. Those are relatively bounded tasks where a human researcher can check the output. You can then use what you learn from that process to tackle tasks that are harder to evaluate.

The important distinction is that producing something that sounds like good alignment research isn’t the same as making progress on alignment. So we need to figure out how to give feedback that rewards the latter. How do you catch subtle mistakes? How do you get the system to explain its uncertainty, rather than just give you an answer you’ll like?

Ideally, this becomes a feedback loop: better alignment methods let us build more useful research assistants, and those assistants help us develop better alignment methods. But we have to keep checking that the loop is producing work we can trust.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few ways. One is that if we want to use AI systems to help us with alignment research, we need to be able to get useful work out of them reliably. So a lot of the things we’re working on today — getting models to follow instructions, getting them to give honest answers, understanding when they’re making things up — are directly relevant to that.

And then alignment research is itself a useful testing ground. Can the model help you find a flaw in an argument? Can it help you design an experiment, or write the code to run it? Initially, you can check those contributions yourself. You can build up from tasks where you have a pretty good ability to evaluate the answer to tasks where evaluating the answer is more difficult.

The thing we ultimately need, though, is more than a model that produces answers we like. We want it to help us notice where our own understanding is wrong, including when that’s something we wouldn’t have thought to ask about. So working on current systems gives us a way to start studying that problem empirically, while the systems are still limited enough that we can do a lot of the checking ourselves.
